content: 1. Specific relaxation therapies have unclear benefits in managing cardiovascular health or related conditions. 2. Most clinical guidelines recommend combining multiple preventive strategies to address cardiovascular risk factors effectively. 3. However, the evidence was insufficient to draw firm conclusions about their effects on cardiovascular events and mortality. 4. For adults without a known diagnosis of hypertension, diabetes, hyperlipidemia, or cardiovascular disease, routine counseling to improve diet and increase physical activity has not been shown to significantly alter behavior and is therefore not recommended. 5. Another Cochrane Review suggested that providing individuals with a cardiovascular disease risk score might slightly reduce cardiovascular risk factors compared to usual care. However, there is uncertainty about whether these scores have any effect on cardiovascular events. 6. It remains unclear whether dental care in individuals with periodontitis affects their risk of cardiovascular disease. 7. A diet rich in fruits and vegetables is associated with a decreased risk of cardiovascular disease and mortality. 8. 9. However, its long-term benefits outside clinical trial settings remain uncertain. 10. A high-fiber diet appears to lower cardiovascular risk. 11. Total fat intake does not seem to be a significant risk factor for cardiovascular disease. 12. Diets high in trans fatty acids increase the rates of cardiovascular disease. 13. Global dietary guidelines recommend reducing saturated fat intake, but there is ongoing debate in the medical literature about the effect of saturated fat on cardiovascular disease. 14. Reviews from 2014 and 2015 did not find evidence of harm from saturated fats. 15. A 2012 Cochrane Review found suggestive evidence of a small benefit from replacing dietary saturated fat with unsaturated fat. 16. A 2013 meta-analysis concluded that substituting omega-6 linoleic acid (a type of unsaturated fat) for saturated fat might increase cardiovascular risk. 17. Replacing saturated fats with carbohydrates does not reduce and may even increase cardiovascular risk. 18. Replacing saturated fats with polyunsaturated fats appears to provide the greatest benefit. However, supplementation with omega-3 fatty acids does not seem to have a significant effect. 19. The effect of a low-salt diet on cardiovascular health is unclear. 20. 21. The same review suggested that a low-salt diet might be harmful in individuals with congestive heart failure. However, this conclusion was criticized for including a trial where participants had low salt and water levels due to diuretics. Excluding this study showed a trend toward benefit in the remaining trials. 22. 23. Moderate evidence indicates that high salt intake increases cardiovascular mortality, and some evidence links it to higher overall mortality, strokes, and left ventricular hypertrophy. 24. 25. Commonly used antihypertensive drug regimens have similar efficacy in reducing the risk of major cardiovascular events, though specific drugs may differ in their ability to prevent certain outcomes. 26. 27. Statins are effective in preventing further cardiovascular events in individuals with a history of cardiovascular disease. 28. Since event rates are higher in men than women, the reduction in events is more apparent in men. 29. In individuals at risk but without a history of cardiovascular disease (primary prevention), statins reduce the risk of death and combined fatal and non-fatal cardiovascular events. 30. U.S. guidelines recommend statins for individuals with a 12% or greater 10-year risk of cardiovascular disease. 31. Niacin, fibrates, and CETP inhibitors, while increasing HDL cholesterol, do not reduce cardiovascular disease risk in individuals already on statins. 32. Anti-diabetic medications may reduce cardiovascular risk in individuals with Type 2 diabetes, but the evidence is inconclusive. 33. A 2009 meta-analysis involving 27,049 participants and 2,370 major vascular events showed a 15% relative risk reduction in cardiovascular disease with more intensive glucose lowering over an average follow-up of 4.4 years, but with an increased risk of major hypoglycemia. 34. Aspirin provides only modest benefit in individuals at low risk of heart disease, as the risk of serious bleeding nearly offsets the cardiovascular benefit. 35. Aspirin is not recommended for individuals at very low risk of cardiovascular disease. 36. The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force advises against aspirin use for prevention in women under 55 and men under 45 years old. However, it may be recommended for older individuals in certain cases. 37. The use of vasoactive agents in individuals with pulmonary hypertension due to left heart disease or hypoxemic lung diseases may cause harm and unnecessary expense. 38. Physical inactivity is estimated to account for 6% of the global burden of coronary heart disease. 39. In Europe, 121,000 deaths from coronary heart disease in 2008 could have been prevented if physical inactivity had been eliminated. 40. 41. While a healthy diet is beneficial, antioxidant supplementation (e.g., vitamin E, vitamin C) or other vitamins has not been shown to protect against cardiovascular disease and may, in some cases, cause harm. 42. Mineral supplements have also not been found to be useful in preventing cardiovascular disease. 43. Niacin (vitamin B3) may modestly reduce the risk of cardiovascular events in high-risk individuals. 44. 45. Magnesium therapy is recommended for individuals with ventricular arrhythmias associated with torsades de pointes and long QT syndrome, as well as for treating arrhythmias caused by digoxin toxicity. 46. There is no evidence to support omega-3 fatty acid supplementation for cardiovascular disease prevention. 47. Cardiovascular disease is treatable, with initial management focusing primarily on dietary and lifestyle interventions. 48. Influenza may exacerbate heart conditions.
